dialogs.title: Dialogue — Middag hos Elin
dialogs.intro: Saturday evening. Elin has invited Dian to dinner at her parents' apartment in Vasastan. Dian is standing at the door with a bunch of flowers.

notes: **The command form comes from the basic form, not from the present tense.** *Att komma* → *kom!*, *att sitta* → *sitt!*, *att ta* → *ta!*. In group 1 the command is exactly the same as the basic form: *att tala* → *tala!*, *att titta* → *titta!*. In the other groups you drop the ending.

**Slå dig ner** literally means "strike yourself down" — a fixed phrase meaning "have a seat". Together with *sätt dig* (sit down) and *ta för dig* (help yourself), these are the three phrases you will hear most often the moment you step into a Swedish home.

**Taking off your shoes is a must.** All over Sweden, shoes are left by the door — in houses, in apartments, often even in small offices. Asking *ska jag ta av mig skorna?* is always safe, and the answer is almost always yes. Tidy socks matter far more in Sweden than in most other countries.

**Varsågod** (say **vah-shoh-GOOD**) is one word that covers three situations: "please, go ahead" when inviting someone, "here you are" when handing something over, and "you're welcome" in reply to thanks. The plural is *varsågoda* when you speak to several people.

**Tack för maten** must be said after a meal in someone's home, by everyone who ate, without exception. Swedish children are taught it from the age of three. Skipping it gets noticed — not as rudeness, but as something odd.

**Skulle du kunna…?** is the most polite way to ask for something in Swedish, a close match for English "would you be able to…?". It is two steps politer than *kan du…?* and is used for requests that really put someone out.

grammars.title: The command form by verb group
after: The rule fits in one sentence: **group 1 uses the basic form as it is; the other groups drop the final *-a***. Since group 1 is the biggest group, most Swedish commands end in *-a*.

To make a command negative, put *inte* **after** the verb: *Glöm inte!* (don't forget!), *Gå inte!* (don't go!), *Oroa dig inte!* (don't worry!). There is no helper like English "don't" — just the verb plus *inte*: literally "forget not!", the way Shakespeare might have said it.

A bare Swedish command sounds **much blunter** than you might expect. *Kom hit!* is an order, not an invitation. For everyday requests to people you don't know well, a question is almost always the better choice.

grammars.title: Five levels of politeness

head: Pattern
Example
Tone
rows: an order — for children, close friends, emergencies
neutral — in a shop, in class
normal and safe — your default choice
very polite — for a big favor
polite but firm — notices and signs

after: The third row is your default. When in doubt, use *kan du…?* — it is right in nine situations out of ten, and never sounds rude or over the top.

Notice that **none of them uses a word for "please"** — because Swedish doesn't really have one. Where English leans on "please", Swedish carries politeness in the shape of the sentence and in *tack*, not in a single magic word.

blocks.text: **Tack för senast** deserves its own explanation: if someone has had you over, you say it again **the next time you see them**, whenever that is — a week later, a month later. It is a very Swedish habit and people notice it; leaving it out makes you seem unappreciative of their hospitality.

blocks.title: Be on time
items: If the invitation says 6:00 p.m., arrive at 6:00 — not 6:20. Fifteen minutes late counts as genuinely late in Sweden, and your host will usually have timed the food to the minute.
Arriving **early** is not polite either. If you happen to get there ten minutes early, wait outside.
Your lifesaver if you are late: **Förlåt att jag är sen!** — Sorry I'm late!

blocks.text: **En kanelbulle** — a sweet rolled bun filled with cinnamon — is the star of the Swedish *fika* table, and it even has its own national day every October 4. If you are invited for *fika*, bringing a bag of *bullar* from the bakery is always welcome.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 11
items: Name ten places in town from Unit 11, each with its preposition: *på banken*, *i affären*, and so on.
Then turn them into commands: *Gå till banken!*, *Titta i affären!*, *Vänta vid kyrkan!*
Finally, soften all five into questions: *Kan du gå till banken?*
